claims.text: The initial material consists of W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial W–Cu composite is prone to phase separation.
The initial W–Cu composite is prone to interfacial void formation.
A pre-added Ti-rich interdendritic phase can serve as a sacrificial phase during liquid-metal dealloying in molten Cu.
Liquid-metal dealloying in molten Cu selectively dissolves the Ti-rich interdendritic channels.
Selective removal of the Ti-rich channels reorganizes the W phase into an aligned structure.
Selective removal of the Ti-rich channels produces a more continuous network of W ligaments within the Cu matrix.
The aligned, continuous W-ligament network reduces phase separation.
The reconfigured W network minimizes interfacial void formation.
Reduced interfacial void content and improved W/Cu continuity create better thermal-conduction pathways.
The dealloyed composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated W–Cu composite.
The predicted thermal-conductivity improvement will persist under thermal cycling representative of W-based plasma-facing-material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
The predicted microstructural and thermal-conductivity improvements will persist under moderate irradiation.
The dealloying temperature must be high enough to enable selective removal of the Ti-rich channels.
Dealloying temperature and time must be controlled to avoid unwanted matrix coarsening.
The untreated W–Cu composite develops significant interfacial voids under service conditions.
Effectiveness under irradiation more extreme than the stated moderate regime has not been established.
The processing time, temperature, and sacrificial-phase content required for an optimal microstructure have not been established.
